{{Short description|Mathematical sequence}}
In [[mathematics]], a '''Weyl sequence''' is a sequence from the [[equidistribution theorem]] proven by [[Hermann Weyl]]:<ref>{{cite journal|last=Weyl|first=H.| author-link=Hermann Weyl |title=Über die Gleichverteilung von Zahlen mod. Eins |trans-title=On the uniform distribution of numbers modulo one |language=de |journal=Mathematische Annalen |date=September 1916 |volume=77|pages=313–352 | doi = 10.1007/BF01475864 | issue = 3|s2cid=123470919|url=https://zenodo.org/record/2425535}}</ref>

The sequence of all multiples of an irrational ''α'',
::0, ''α'', 2''α'', 3''α'', 4''α'', ...
:is [[Continuous uniform distribution|equidistributed]] modulo 1.<ref>{{cite book | first1=L. | last1=Kuipers | first2=H. | last2=Niederreiter |author2-link = Harald Niederreiter | title=Uniform Distribution of Sequences | publisher=Dover Publications | year=2006 | orig-year=1974 | isbn=0-486-45019-8 }}</ref>

In other words, the sequence of the fractional parts of each term will be uniformly distributed in the interval&nbsp;[0,&nbsp;1).

== In computing ==
In [[computing]], an integer version of this sequence is often used to generate a [[discrete uniform distribution]] rather than a continuous one.   Instead of using an irrational number, which cannot be calculated on a digital computer, the ratio of two integers is used in its place.  An integer ''k'' is chosen, [[relatively prime]] to an integer modulus ''m''.  In the common case that ''m'' is a power of 2, this amounts to requiring that ''k'' is odd.<!-- It's not technically required that 0 < k < m, since only the residue class of k matters.-->

The sequence of all multiples of such an integer ''k'',
::0, ''k'', 2''k'', 3''k'', 4''k'', …                           
: is equidistributed modulo ''m''.

That is, the sequence of the remainders of each term when divided by ''m'' will be uniformly distributed in the interval {{nowrap begin}}[0, ''m''{{nowrap end}}).

The term appears to originate with [[George Marsaglia]]’s paper "[[Xorshift]] RNGs".<ref name="marsaglia">{{cite journal
| first=George | last=Marsaglia | author-link=George Marsaglia 
| title=Xorshift RNGs
| journal=[[Journal of Statistical Software]]
| volume=8 | issue=14
| date=July 2003
| url=http://www.jstatsoft.org/v08/i14/paper | doi=10.18637/jss.v008.i14| doi-access=free}}</ref> 
The following C code generates what Marsaglia calls a "Weyl sequence":
::d += 362437;
In this case, the odd integer is 362437, and the results are computed modulo {{nowrap|1=''m'' = 2<sup>''32''</sup>}} because d is a 32-bit quantity. The results are equidistributed modulo 2<sup>32</sup>.
